tombstone: Rustam Takes Aim at Ashkabus, from a Shah-nama (Book of Kings), c. 1425–50. Sultanate India, Deccan or Malwa. Gum tempera and ink on paper; folio: 31.8 x 25.6 cm (12 1/2 x 10 1/16 in.); painting: 13.7 x 20.5 cm (5 3/8 x 8 1/16 in.). The Cleveland Museum of Art, Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund, 2020.204
title: Rustam Takes Aim at Ashkabus, from a Shah-nama (Book of Kings)
technique: Gum tempera and ink on paper

inscriptions.inscription:
The heavens themselves echo the action of the arrow;/ 
Fate said “Take it!” and Fortune nodded “Give!”/ 
The Heavens cried, “Excellent!” and the Moon said “Well Done!”
inscriptions.inscription_remark: On top of the page in black script in the margin is a famous line which occurs in some manuscripts but is relegated to footnotes by those who regard it as a later interpolation, although it has become proverbially popular.

did_you_know: In the upside-down inscription in the top margin: The Heavens cried, “Excellent!” and the Moon said “Well Done!”
description: The central warrior is Iran’s mythic hero Rustam, who approached an enemy army on foot, aiming to shoot the general off his mount. This page is from the oldest surviving illustrated Islamic manuscript made in India. The painting is by a local artist working for a Sultanate patron in India who admired Persian literature and emulated the erudite court culture of Iran.
